claims.text: Adding aluminum to DC magnetron-sputtered TiCrZrNbTa coatings will promote formation of an alumina scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The resulting alumina scale will be stable, continuous, and adherent.
Increasing aluminum content will improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of TiCrZrNbTa-coated zirconium-alloy cladding.
The aluminum-enhanced coating can retain suitability for nuclear-fuel-cladding service.
During high-temperature exposure, aluminum preferentially oxidizes to Al2O3.
A dense Al2O3 layer limits oxygen diffusion into the underlying metal.
Limiting oxygen diffusion reduces the overall oxidation rate.
The protective alumina layer will maintain coating integrity under service conditions.
Relative to baseline TiCrZrNbTa, aluminum-enhanced coatings will have lower oxidation-associated weight gain.
Relative to baseline TiCrZrNbTa, aluminum-enhanced coatings will exhibit better oxide-scale adherence.
Relative to baseline TiCrZrNbTa, aluminum-enhanced coatings will exhibit less oxide spallation.
A TiCrZrNbTa coating with no or minimal aluminum has higher oxidation rates and forms a less protective oxide scale under comparable conditions.
An optimum aluminum range, likely a few atomic percent, can enable alumina formation without significantly degrading thermal expansion behavior, adhesion, or mechanical strength.
Extremely high aluminum levels may cause phase instability or embrittlement and limit the oxidation benefit.
